questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Why a circular orbit admits one speed only
questions.learningObjective: explain why a circular orbit fixes a unique speed
questions.stem: A designer claims a probe will hold a circular orbit at 7.0e6 m from a planet's centre at whatever speed it happens to be travelling. Using the circular-orbit condition, explain why that claim cannot be right.

answer.exemplar: In a circular orbit the only real force is gravity, and it must supply the whole centripetal acceleration, so the field strength at that radius, G M over r squared, must equal v squared over r. Dividing through leaves the speed equal to the square root of G M over r, which fixes one speed and no other for a given radius. Travelling faster than that means the path curves less sharply than the circle does, so the probe swings outward into a larger orbit, while travelling slower means the path curves more sharply, so the probe drops inward toward the planet. The satellite's own mass cancels from the condition entirely, so no amount of mass rescues the claim.

questions.explanation: A complete answer writes the condition equating the field to v squared over r, solves it to show a single speed, and explains that speeds above and below it lead to outward and inward motion respectively, noting that the satellite's mass drops out of the relation.
questions.hint: Set gravity equal to the required centripetal acceleration and see how many solutions result.
